c11_eng_w_cbse_06_014: Retelling isn't writing — pick a persona and the evidence for the purpose. Check: what's the task asking?
c11_eng_w_cbse_06_015: Consensus isn't the goal — the prompts invite genuine disagreement with evidence. Check: what's your counter-reading?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_001: The famine isn't a date — it explains why Satyajit can't confess his ruin. Check: what pressure shapes him?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_002: The train is the frame, the forger memory a flashback — and the deed-signing is the real climax. Check: which peak resolves him?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_003: Mud bricks and brass bowls build the reverence he can't deserve. Check: what do the details do?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_004: He isn't just a victim — his glory rose on a forger's trembling hand. Check: where was he complicit?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_005: Srinath, Harish, Beena each embody a force — patronage, predation, ritual. Check: which theme does each carry?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_006: 'Banking failure' is a topic — the theme is what ruin does to dignity. Check: stated or explored?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_007: The wedding is the stage — transactional relationships are the theme playing on it. Check: element or idea?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_008: 'Wheel of fortune' maps fate's cycles onto his career — imagery alone equates nothing. Check: mapping or picture?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_009: A stopped train isn't ironic — glory built on a forgery is. Check: what expectation broke?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_010: 'Queer' here means strange — the head-wagging is grief, not excitement. Check: which era's meaning?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_011: The fragment 'of which he had attained control' enacts the mental fragmentation. Check: what does the break do?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_012: 'He was kind' needs the 'daughter crisis' monologue behind it. Check: which inner line?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_013: His final silence isn't nobility — it can read as complicity in performative giving. Check: how is it built?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_014: Don't retell the theft — analyse how it comments on his success. Check: method or event?
c11_eng_w_cbse_07_015: 'He was too proud' needs the homage-craving line to hold. Check: interpretation or projection?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_001: Maugham's medical training and the franc's value set the tension — the preview is a lens. Check: what does it predict?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_002: The whole lunch is a flashback inside a twenty-year frame — the ending is the revenge. Check: why twenty years later?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_003: The atmosphere isn't his fear — the menu prices build the dread. Check: feeling or created mood?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_004: He isn't a pushover — the courtesy is strategy, and his thoughts are razor-sharp. Check: compliance or control?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_005: She talks more but he owns the lens — even the 'priest-like' waiter is his projection. Check: whose consciousness?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_006: 'Lunch' is a topic — the theme is pretension masking exploitation, told through his mockery. Check: topic or claim?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_007: The gods take the hand, not him — the revenge is ironic, not ethical. Check: judgment or observation?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_008: Butter smells and 'tickled nostrils' are imagery — and 'Jehovah' mocks her piety. Check: which sense?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_009: Her 'one thing' line against her orders is verbal irony — the chop is just a cheap meal. Check: which type?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_010: 'Caviare' isn't 'fish eggs' — it performs her casual luxury. Check: what does the choice stage?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_011: 'I never eat more than one thing' repeated with exceptions is hypocrisy built in grammar. Check: what does repetition do?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_012: 'Greedy' needs the caviar-asparagus-peach sequence behind it. Check: what's the chain?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_013: Her claim vs her eating is verbal; his ruin is situational; our early suspicion is dramatic. Check: which is which?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_014: Quotes must be woven in — 'I never eat more than one thing' inside your sentence. Check: block or thread?
c11_eng_w_cbse_08_015: Answer the last speaker with a reference — 'after claiming she never eats...' Check: whose point did you extend?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_001: 'A peacock visits' is the poem's story — context is who wrote it, when and why. Check: content or conditions?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_002: The poem's arc is conditional setup, sensory cascade, metaphor — not a plot. Check: what resolves it?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_003: The colours aren't the setting — they're the atmosphere materialising through his attention. Check: what does perception build?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_004: The peacock isn't proud — its beauty is camouflage for reluctance. Check: display or withdrawal?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_005: The cat has no backstory — it stretches once to mark the peacock's presence. Check: function or biography?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_006: The beauty isn't the theme — the paradox of attention is. Check: subject or insight?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_007: 'Turquoise' is a motif — 'patience reveals beauty' is a theme. Check: image or insight?
c11_eng_w_cbse_09_008: 'Loud sharp call' is auditory imagery — and the metaphors build elusiveness. Check: what work does it do?
